posts.title: MSI tables land in the generator
posts.description: msi-generator v0.2 writes real OLE2 compound files, cabinets, and core Windows Installer tables — still unsigned, no longer an empty stub.
posts.html:
msi-generator crossed the line from “skeleton that prints a message” to “file you can open in an OLE/MSI viewer.”

v0.2 writes a version-3 compound file, an uncompressed cabinet payload, and the core table set (Directory, Component, File, Feature, FeatureComponents, Property, Media, plus _Tables / _Columns and the string pool). MSIX gained multi-file payloads and placeholder assets so manifests stop lying about missing logos.

This is the engine Easy Installer’s msi / msix plugins call. It is not WiX, and we are not pretending a unsigned sample MSI is Store-ready — but the binary formats are finally real enough to iterate on.

Release: v0.2.0 · docs: component.

posts.title: Easy Installer ships
posts.description: A CLI and Explorer menu for installer projects and Install in-place PATH — without waiting on a full MSI every time you want a tool on PATH.
posts.html:
We shipped Easy Installer: the host that turns “put this folder on PATH” and “build an installer from this tree” into something you can right-click or script.

The first beat is deliberately small. Install in-place (add to PATH) means what it says — append the folder to the user PATH, keep a ledger so you can undo, and skip the copy-into-Program-Files ritual when you are iterating on a CLI. File Explorer gets a menu for it (Win11 modern when the sparse package builds; classic cascade otherwise). Linux and macOS get file-manager actions too.

The second beat is the project file. installer.kdl plus plugins: portable zip always works; NSIS and Inno emit scripts and call their compilers when present; MSI/MSIX call msi-generator; AppImage gets a stub path on Linux. Optional designer GUIs are discoverable (plugins install-gui) instead of reinvented inside our IDE.

DevCentr picks up the same verbs — New → Installer Project, toolbar Install in-place PATH, and CLI modes — so the OS menu and the app are not two products pretending to be one.

Docs: Easy Installer (once the hub rebuilds) · releases.

posts.title: We’re partnering with OpenShellOrg (on purpose)
posts.description: DevCentr and OpenShellOrg are locking in the sibling story—toolchain ownership on our side, shell entrypoint honesty on theirs.
posts.html:
Quick confession: for a minute we almost convinced ourselves the whole “wrong Node / wrong Flutter / wrong host” rant lived under OpenShellOrg, because that’s where the pain hits—you type a command and the wrong process runs. Then we remembered why we put Toolchain Management in DevCentr in the first place: the full lifecycle (pin, health, repair, upgrade) is an ecosystem-orchestration problem. The shell just happens to be the crime scene.

So we’re doing the grown-up thing.

DevCentr keeps the canonical Toolchain Management Pattern → Protocol → Control Plane → TCF kit. That’s the “official entrypoint owns the lifecycle” philosophy, the advisories in Ecosystem Management, the “stop telling newcomers to go shop for nvm/FVM first” stance.

OpenShellOrg keeps the shell-boundary essay: Entrypoint Dispatch — auto-install and re-exec the right host/version when the pin says so — plus nu-require, SOS, structured-shell thesis, env-refresh / shell-host plans. Complementary. Not a duplicate manifesto with a different logo.

Aligned, not merged. Cross-linked like we mean it. Footers and org profiles now show the sibling cluster so people stop spelunking.

If you want the vibe in one line: we orchestrate the workshop; they refuse to let the hammer lie about which nail it’s hitting.

posts.title: We’re opening a News desk
posts.description: Why DevCentr is starting a public News feed—and what you won't find here.
posts.html:
Dev-Centr has been shipping in public for a while—docs, tools, the app, the whole messy orbit of related projects. What we haven’t had is a place to talk about that work like people talk about it: the why, the bets, the “here’s where we’re headed” pieces.

So we’re starting News at devcentr.org/news.

Think magazine column more than release notes. If something changes how we build, how we show up as an org, or what we’re trying to become, it belongs here. If it’s “we fixed a heading and renamed three pages,” that’s the Changelog.

We’ll write when there’s something worth saying. No weekly quota. No content mill. Subscribe to the RSS or Atom feed if you want a ping when we do.

Elsewhere, as always: the docs, the repos, and the app.

posts.title: Stop dumping people into the docs
posts.description: We built a Help hub so “I need assistance” doesn't mean “go read the manual.”
posts.html:
Here’s a quiet failure mode a lot of open projects share: someone shows up stuck, and the only door we offer is documentation. Docs are great when you want to learn. They’re a cold shoulder when you want a person—or at least a clear path to one.

So we put up a Help hub at devcentr.org/help.

The idea is simple. Help is the umbrella. Under it you can choose self-help (docs, guides, the knowledge base) or support (talk to us). Status and community channels sit next to both, so you’re not hunting through the footer for Slack or “is the site up?”

We don’t have a polished ticket desk yet—and we’re not going to pretend we do. For now, mail support@devcentr.org. A real assisted desk (tickets, maybe AI triage) is on the roadmap; we’d rather ship an honest front door than a half-built system with a shiny button.

If you just want the pulse of our public surfaces, /status runs live probes. Longer uptime history still lives at status.devcentr.org.

This is a small change on the site. It’s a bigger change in posture: we assume visitors arrive with different jobs to do, and we stop treating “read the docs” as the only answer.

posts.title: Our logo shouldn’t need a proprietary player
posts.description: Why DevCentr's new mark stays in SVG—and why we're cautious about Rive as a default for open brands.
posts.html:
We finally gave DevCentr a proper mark: an orbital hub that reads as a center of gravity. You’ll see it on the site, in the GitHub avatar, and in the motion loop that doesn’t need JavaScript to breathe.

That last part matters more than it sounds.

There’s a loud fashion in product design right now: ship brand motion as a black-box file, drop in a player, call it modern. Rive is genuinely good at interactive chrome—state machines, theme hooks, the works. Its runtimes are open. The editor isn’t, and the .riv format is binary. That means weak git diffs and a hard wall for anyone (human or agent) who wants to edit the motion as text.

We’re building an open ecosystem. Our logo shouldn’t be the one asset that only opens in a paid app.

So the default for portable marks stays animated SVG and CSS. Lottie when you’ve got a baked After Effects timeline. Rive when you’re already deep in interactive app UI and the player is justified. We’re documenting those lanes in General Knowledge; the short version is: don’t hard-advocate a proprietary editor as the open standard for brand motion.

Longer term we want something text-first that agents can actually edit. Popkorn is an early CSS-shaped candidate—interesting, not a Dev-Centr default yet. If that future interests you, there’s an open thread on rich interactivity at ayarse/popkorn#7.

The mark is the visible change. The opinion underneath it is the story: open brands should travel as open source.
